Series::LinearAlgAccessor::mm¶

Back to Series::LinearAlgAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series Series::LinearAlgAccessor::mm(const Series& other) const
Series SeriesLinearAlgProxy::mm() const
Series Series::mm(const Series& other) const

What It Does¶

mm() performs one matrix-matrix multiplication and requires both operands to be two-dimensional. If the left matrix has shape [m, k] and the right matrix has shape [k, n], the result has shape [m, n]:

out[i, j] = sum(left[i, t] * right[t, j], over t)

The shared k dimension disappears because it is summed. The left row count m and right column count n survive. Rectangular matrices are therefore normal: mm() does not mean “square matrix multiplication.”

Rows Against Columns¶

Read the operation as a table of row-column inner products. Every output row comes from one row of the left matrix; every output column comes from one column of the right matrix. The entry at [i, j] answers: “how strongly does left row i align with right column j?”

Use mm() rather than matmul() when rank 2 is part of the program’s contract. A vector or batch then fails immediately instead of silently selecting a different rank rule.

Parameter¶

other (const Series&) The right-hand matrix. It must have rank 2, use the same dtype and platform as the left matrix, and satisfy left.size(1) == other.size(0).

Returns¶

Series A new rank-2 Series with shape [left.size(0), other.size(1)]. Neither operand is modified.

Gradient¶

For C = A B and incoming sensitivity G = dL/dC, reverse mode applies:

dL/dA = G B^T
dL/dB = A^T G

The transpose turns output-space sensitivity back toward each input’s shape. For complex matrices, the corresponding adjoint uses conjugate transposes.

Examples¶

Example 1. The accessor accepts either a method argument or a peer bound when the proxy is created. Both forms keep left as the left operand.

auto left = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto right = pluss::make_series({{2.0, 0.0}, {1.0, 2.0}});

std::cout << "peer_argument=" << left.linearalg.mm(right) << "\n";
std::cout << "peer_bound=" << left.linearalg(right).mm() << "\n";

The first output entry is the first left row dotted with the first right column: 1*2 + 2*1 = 4.

Output¶

peer_argument=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[4, 4],
  [10, 8]]
peer_bound=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[4, 4],
  [10, 8]]

Example 2. Rectangular dimensions determine the result shape. A [2, 3] matrix multiplied by a [3, 2] matrix returns [2, 2].

auto left = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 0.0, 2.0},
    {-1.0, 3.0, 1.0},
});
auto right = pluss::make_series({
    {3.0, 1.0},
    {1.0, 2.0},
    {2.0, 0.0},
});

std::cout << left.linearalg.mm(right) << "\n";

For the second row and second column, (-1)*1 + 3*2 + 1*0 = 5.

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[7, 1],
  [2, 5]]

Example 3. Track both matrices through a scalar objective.

auto left = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto right = pluss::make_series({{5.0, 6.0}, {7.0, 8.0}});
left.tracks_slope_(true);
right.tracks_slope_(true);

left.linearalg.mm(right).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "dL_dleft=" << left.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dright=" << right.sensitivity() << "\n";

Summing the output supplies an all-ones incoming matrix. Each left row gets the right matrix’s row sums [11, 15]; each right column gets the left matrix’s column sums [4, 6].

Output¶

dL_dleft=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[11, 15],
  [11, 15]]
dL_dright=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[4, 4],
  [6, 6]]

Example 4 (contract check). A vector on either side is not accepted, even if its length would fit an equivalent matmul() expression.

try {
  auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
  std::cout << matrix.linearalg.mm(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0})) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << e.what() << "\n";
}

Output¶

mm: expected two 2D Series

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Both operands must have rank 2; mm() never broadcasts batches.

  • left.size(1) must equal other.size(0).

  • Dtypes and platforms must match.

  • Matrix multiplication is order-sensitive: A.mm(B) and B.mm(A) need not have the same shape or values.

  • Use mul() for position-by-position multiplication.

Summary¶

mm() is the contract-first matrix product. It contracts columns of the left matrix against rows of the right and always returns a rank-2 matrix.
